author: agenticbranduniverse.com/registry
description: A scene separated into depth planes that move at different rates as the page scrolls. The content is not any one plane; it is the ORDER. One flat plate drifting is a texture. Three planes moving at different rates is depth.

schemaNotes.z: Depth index. 0 is furthest from the viewer.
schemaNotes.speed: Fraction of page scroll this plane keeps up with. Lower is further away. It LAGS by (1 - speed).
schemaNotes.alpha: true if the plane is a cutout. Exactly one plane may be false, and it must be the backmost.
schemaNotes.anchor: top | bottom. Which edge of the frame the plane is pinned to.
schemaNotes.fit: width | height. 'width' spans the frame (a skyline band, a sky). 'height' is sized by heightFrac and centred (a group of figures).
schemaNotes.heightFrac: For fit: height — the plane's height as a fraction of the frame. Depth alone does not say how BIG a thing is, and a plane sized only by its render's aspect will happily swallow every plane behind it.
schemaNotes.subject: What is in the plane. This is the prompt's subject line, kept so the plane can be re-rendered.
schemaNotes.offsetVh: Lift a bottom-anchored plane off the frame floor, in vh. Depth alone does not place a plane: without this every bottom plane shares one baseline, so the nearest one simply buries the rest and the middle planes have nothing to do. Lifting a far plane is what puts it somewhere it can be seen first and occluded second, which is the gesture the whole scene exists for.
schemaNotes.depthFade: Aerial perspective, 0..1, where 1 is untouched. Distance drains contrast and light, so a far plane rendered at full strength does two bad things at once: it stops reading as far, and it competes with everything in front of it — including the copy. Snow-lit peaks were the BRIGHTEST thing on the page while being the furthest, which is backwards, and no amount of text-shadow fixes a background that is brighter than the text.
schemaNotes.minHeightVh: Floor on the plane's height, in vh. A width-fitted band is sized by the frame's WIDTH while every offset here is in vh, so rotating to portrait shrinks the band roughly fourfold while its offset does not move. Past this floor the plane covers by HEIGHT and overflows sideways, which is free because the frame already clips that axis. One value, no breakpoint: on a wide frame the width fit already exceeds the floor and it does nothing.
schemaNotes.mobileHidden: Drop the plane on narrow frames. BANDS survive portrait once they have a minHeightVh; small centred OBJECTS do not, because a narrow frame has no clear air to hang them in and they land on the copy. Cut objects, keep bands — cutting bands too drops the plane count far enough that the scene stops reading as layered at all.

slots.trim: Every alpha plane is trimmed to its own alpha bounding box before it is sized. An untrimmed cutout is mostly empty pixels, so 'height' means the height of the EMPTY RECTANGLE rather than of the thing, and every size is a lie.

generators.note: A plane whose content is procedural (a starfield, a grid, a horizon) should be DRAWN by a §4.11 generator rather than rendered. Its keep-out regions stay numbers instead of hopes.

perSlot.assert: no green rim and no glowing veil, proofed on BOTH a light and a dark ground. Checking one ground is how a halo ships: a light ground hides excess coverage, a dark ground hides dark contamination.
no floor, contact shadow, reflection or horizon inside the cutout. A plane that carries its own ground cannot sit in front of another plane.

perSlot.scope: every plane with alpha: true, on the edge that faces the viewer's side of the frame
perSlot.assert: the plane's own rectangle must be undetectable, and on a trimmed cutout the trim itself is the danger: trimming to the alpha box leaves whatever the render cut off sitting on a dead straight line. Break it with CONTENT — a ragged treeline, a crowd of varied heights, a broken parapet — so there is no straight edge to find. Reach for a mask only when content cannot do it, because a mask that hides an edge also thins the thing it is hiding, and a far plane made ghostly stops reading as far and starts reading as faded.

crossSlot.assert: speed increases strictly with z. If it does not, the illusion inverts and the scene reads as broken rather than as flat.
at most one plane is opaque. Two opaque planes means the front one hides everything behind it.
the opaque plane, if any, is the one with the lowest z. An opaque plane anywhere but the back is a wall.

crossSlot.scope: all planes composited in z order
crossSlot.assert: the planes read as one coherent scene, in one light, at one time of day — not as separate images stacked.
under prefers-reduced-motion every plane freezes, and the still composition must look deliberate rather than merely acceptable.

crossSlot.scope: all alpha planes, compared to each other
crossSlot.assert: contrast and brightness fall off with distance: no alpha plane may be more contrasty than a plane in front of it. Judged rather than computed because the backmost plane is legitimately exempt — a starfield DRAWN by a generator is already authored at its final contrast and is not 'faded', it is dark.

crossSlot.scope: any copy laid over the scene, at every scroll position
crossSlot.assert: In a static hero you can place text over a dark patch and be done. Here the art MOVES, so every line passes over every plane eventually — text placed against one plane WILL end up on another. Copy must carry its own legibility (its own halo, and a colour that is not near any plane's), and it must never be rescued with a scrim over the art, which puts a rectangle back on the scene.

crossSlot.scope: the whole scene at portrait aspect
crossSlot.assert: the plane carrying the SUBJECT is visible without scrolling. Geometry tuned at one aspect ratio does not survive the other: the first portrait build pushed the rooftop — the entire point of the scene — below the fold and left only atmosphere on screen, which is a scene about nothing. Check portrait before shipping, and check it by asking what the visitor SEES, not whether every plane loaded.

placement.note: A projection normally stops at the artifact. This one carries a placement contract because its emitted planes are only correct IN a scrolling page, and every failure below was shipped at least once before it was written down.
rules: The scene lives in ONE frame that starts above the section by the overhang, so every plane's headroom is already inside it. That frame IS clipped, and must be. A positioned section paints above the non-positioned sections that follow it, so a plane allowed to overflow downward lands on top of the next section's copy.

The frame's bottom edge is dissolved ONCE, on the frame. Per-plane fades are wrong here: a plane that sinks carries its own fade down with it, so the clip ends up cutting the opaque part and the hard edge returns.

It resolves to TRANSPARENT, never to a colour. Fading to the page background is correct on exactly one background and a visible plate on every other. See userexperience.wiki/concepts/the-vanishing-edge.
Bottom planes move RELATIVE TO THE NEAREST of them, which therefore never moves. Parallax is relative motion, so this costs nothing visually and guarantees the plane pinned to the floor stays pinned.
Bottom planes need `offsetVh`. Sharing one baseline means the nearest plane simply buries the rest, and the middle planes have nothing to do.

Cap the SCROLL the planes read, not each plane's own shift. Capping shifts freezes the fast-falling planes first, so the planes stop moving relative to each other and the occlusion never happens — the scene goes dead after a fifth of a screen.
Nothing painted over the scene (a bloom, a gradient, a scrim) may have a hard edge of its own. A seam in the composite is usually the overlay, not the planes.

Alpha planes are rendered on FLAT CHROMA GREEN with no shadow, floor or reflection, then keyed with skills/on-brand-image/scripts/chroma_key.py. A warm ground bakes a contact shadow that reads as gold on a gold subject, and no heuristic separates it.
